rows.title: How Jacob Loud's Land Was Lost
rows.standfirst: Today's show: the arcane laws that have cost Black landowners their property, and the lawyer who is trying to fix those laws. | Subscribe to our weekly newsletter here.

rows.title: Indicator Favs: The Rise Of The Machines
rows.standfirst: In today's classic, the robots take over the show from Cardiff and Stacey as we continue our week of favorite episodes.

rows.title: Saks Says No To Fur, The Latest Fashion Seller To Go Fur-Free
rows.standfirst: Saks Fifth Avenue will phase out sales of animal-fur products, joining other retailers such as Macy's that are responding to growing anti-fur sentiment among shoppers.

rows.title: Texas Courts Open Eviction Floodgates: 'We Just Stepped Off A Cliff'
rows.standfirst: Judges in Texas are being told it's not their job to enforce a CDC order aimed at stopping evictions. Housing groups fear that a wave of unnecessary evictions will leave thousands homeless.

rows.title: The Housing Market Is Wild Right Now — And It's Making Inequality Worse
rows.standfirst: Home prices are soaring around the U.S. Amid low inventory and historically low interest rates, some buyers are hitting the market to find they can't compete with all-cash offers, or bidding wars that escalate well out of their price range.

rows.title: Indicator Favs: The Recession Predictor
rows.standfirst: It wouldn't be favorites week at The Indicator without the yield curve. Meet it again for the first time in this classic from the first time Cardiff brought it to the show.

rows.title: Governor Aims To Reopen California By Mid-June, Contingent On Public Health Metrics
rows.standfirst: Gov. Gavin Newsom announced a tentative statewide reopening date of June 15, provided vaccine availability increases and hospitalizations remain low.

rows.title: Rising Tide: Powerful U.S. Growth Set To Lift Global Economy, IMF Says
rows.standfirst: The International Monetary Fund predicts the U.S. economy will grow at its fastest pace in decades this year, lifting the outlook for worldwide economic growth.

rows.title: A Row Over Rare-Earth Deposits Could Bring Down Greenland's Government
rows.standfirst: Greenlanders are going to the polls Tuesday in a crucial election that could determine if the island taps its vast deposits of rare-earth minerals to fuel eventual independence from Denmark.

rows.title: Stranger Danger: An Economist's Guide To Overcoming Distrust
rows.standfirst: A new book delves into humanity's long march to overcoming distrust.

rows.title: New Zealand, Australia To Create 'Travel Bubble,' Resume Quarantine-Free Travel
rows.standfirst: The pandemic is under such control in the two countries that people will be able to travel between them for the first time without quarantining since March 2020.

rows.title: Janet Yellen Proposes Bold Idea: The Same Minimum Corporate Tax Around The World
rows.standfirst: The Treasury secretary is adding her support to a widely discussed proposal as part of the Biden administration's tougher approach to corporate taxes.

rows.title: Indicator Favs: Let's Get Ready To Retail
rows.standfirst: This week we're picking our favorite Indicators and adding a little behind the scenes peek. Today, the first time Stacey and Cardiff realized they share a taste for the bizarre in podcasting.

rows.title: Supreme Court Hands Google A Win Over Oracle In Multibillion-Dollar Case
rows.standfirst: By a 6-to-2 vote, the justices said Google's use of Oracle code did not infringe copyright laws.

rows.title: Group-Chat App Discord Says It Banned More Than 2,000 Extremist Communities
rows.standfirst: The popular platform also reported on Monday that it deleted more than 300 communities, known on the site as "servers," that were dedicated to the conspiracy theory QAnon.

rows.title: Coinbase, A Bitcoin Startup, Goes Public. Is Crypto Really The 'Future Of Finance'?
rows.standfirst: Coinbase's public debut comes as more institutions warm up to the idea of cryptocurrency and its popularity among investors soars.

rows.title: Workin' 9 To 5
rows.standfirst: The movie "9 to 5" used humor to highlight the struggles of women in the workplace 40 years ago. Where are we now? | Subscribe to our weekly newsletter here.

rows.title: Falun Gong, Steve Bannon And The Trump-Era Battle Over Internet Freedom
rows.standfirst: The Trump administration and a Democratic activist fought to win millions in federal funds for anti-censorship software tied to Falun Gong. That saga is now at the center of a criminal investigation.

rows.title: Journalist Investigates 'Crime Story' Of The Sackler Family And The Opioid Crisis
rows.standfirst: Empire of Pain author Patrick Radden Keefe says the Sackler family has "thrown a lot of energy" into trying to thwart his reporting about the family's involvement in the opioid crisis.

rows.title: Do The Golden Arches Bend Toward Justice?
rows.standfirst: Calls for racial justice are met with a lot of different proposals, but one of the loudest and most enduring is to invest in Black businesses. But can "buying Black" actually do anything to mitigate racism? To find out, we're taking a look at the surprising link between Black capitalism and McDonald's.

rows.title: How Burlington Powered Through 2020 Without A Website
rows.standfirst: Burlington shut down its online store right as the pandemic started, but it still weathered 2020 well. In fact, its stock prices just hit an all time high! What's Burlington's secret to success?

rows.title: Hundreds Of Companies Call For U.S. To Slash Carbon Emissions
rows.standfirst: In a move to curb climate change, an open letter from companies including Apple and Walmart calls on the Biden administration to cut U.S. emissions to at least half of 2005 levels by 2030.

rows.title: Consumer Prices Jumped. Should You Worry? That's Sparking A Heated Debate
rows.standfirst: Consumer prices jumped last month as businesses struggled to keep pace with booming demand, but the Biden administration and the Federal Reserve say the uptick in inflation is likely to be temporary.

rows.title: He Tried To Organize Workers In China's Gig Economy. Now He Faces 5 Years In Jail
rows.standfirst: The arrest of food delivery worker Chen Guojiang dealt a blow to nascent efforts to promote couriers' rights as they've gained broader public attention during the coronavirus pandemic.

rows.title: The Biden Administration's Women-Led Push For Investment In 'Care Infrastructure'
rows.standfirst: President Biden wants to make a massive investment in infrastructure, and not just in roads and bridges. His administration is proposing big investments in "care infrastructure" — investments designed to help women succeed in the workforce.

rows.title: How Amazon Defeated The Union
rows.standfirst: The results are in: Amazon workers in Bessemer, Alabama will not unionize, for now. We discuss the tactics companies use to keep organized labor at bay.

rows.title: White House Convenes Summit To Address Supply Shortage Crippling Auto Plants
rows.standfirst: A lack of computer parts known as semiconductors threatens many industries, hitting automakers especially hard. The White House brought together executives from 19 companies to confront the issue.

rows.title: MLB's Move Out Of Georgia Is The Latest In A Line Of Political Boycotts
rows.standfirst: Today's boycotts aren't coming out of nowhere. Here's a look at some prominent examples in history and how boycotts got started.

rows.title: South Korean Electric Vehicle Battery Makers Reach $1.8B Deal To End Trade Dispute
rows.standfirst: The deal means both companies will be able to produce lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles at a time when President Biden hopes to boost support for the industry as part of his climate plan.

rows.title: This Top Biden Economist Has A Plan: Create Jobs, Address Inequality, Ignore Trolls
rows.standfirst: Janelle Jones is the first Black woman to serve as chief economist at the Labor Department. She says helping marginalized groups boosts the entire economy.

rows.title: Faulty Takata Air Bag Blamed For January Death In South Carolina
rows.standfirst: Honda said Wednesday that it had tried more than 100 times to reach owners of the 2002 Accord with recall warnings.

rows.title: The Writers Revolt (UPDATE)
rows.standfirst: We have a winner in an epic Hollywood story. A couple years back, 7,000 TV writers across the U.S. fired their agents. All on the same day. It was part of a battle over how creative work gets valued and compensated in TV and film. Now, we have the dramatic resolution. | Subscribe to our weekly newsletter here.

rows.title: Shuttered Venues Still Waiting For Government Aid Announced In December
rows.standfirst: The Small Business Administration experienced a rough launch for its grant program intended to help long-beleaguered venues. After so long without a lifeline, though, time is running thin.

rows.title: FDA Inspection Finds Numerous Problems At Facility Intended To Make J&J Vaccine
rows.standfirst: The report on Emergent BioSolutions' Baltimore factory found an array of problems, from peeling paint to inadequate measures to prevent cross-contamination. Manufacturing at the facility is on hold.

rows.title: Too Many Real Estate Agents
rows.standfirst: There are now more realtors than homes for sale, and this is not just concerning for real estate agents facing extra competition. New research suggests too many real estate agents can make downturns worse for the entire housing market.

rows.title: 'Project Mayhem': Reporters Race To Save Tribune Papers From 'Vulture' Fund
rows.standfirst: The Baltimore Sun 's Liz Bowie is leading reporters across Tribune properties to find civic-minded owners for the chain's newspapers before a hedge fund with a record of slashing cuts buys the company.

rows.title: Governors Urge Biden To Order 100% Zero-Emission Car Sales By 2035
rows.standfirst: In a letter to the president, 12 governors asked that the White House order a ban on greenhouse gas-emitting cars and light trucks within 14 years.

rows.title: Open Up And Say... 'Huh?': Nashville Venues Grapple With City's Lack Of Reopening Plan
rows.standfirst: WPLN News reports on Nashville's long-suffering live music scene and the city's lack of a cohesive plan.

rows.title: VIDEO: Is Recycling Worth It Anymore? People On The Front Lines Say Maybe Not
rows.standfirst: As America continues to lead the world in per capita waste production, it's becoming more and more clear that everybody — from manufacturers to consumers — "over-believes" in recycling.

rows.title: Some CEOs Are Hearing A New Message: Act On Climate, Or We'll Cut Your Pay
rows.standfirst: Some companies, under pressure from shareholders, are tying executive compensation to climate targets. It's not widespread yet, but the approach is catching on.

rows.title: Far-Right-Friendly Platform Parler Expected To Return To App Store Next Week
rows.standfirst: Apple suspended the platform from its app store in the wake of the Capitol riots, citing inadequate content moderation practices. Parler says it will relaunch next week with "several new safeguards."

rows.title: Plastic Is The New Toilet Paper For Scientists
rows.standfirst: A lot of pandemic-related supply chain snafus have been corrected, but scientists are still struggling to get some of their most basic supplies. What's going on?

rows.title: When You Add More Police To A City, What Happens?
rows.standfirst: A new study looks at the effects of growing police forces on racial inequality.

rows.title: It's Time To Fly
rows.standfirst: People are flying again. But so many airplanes are still parked in storage. Getting them in the air again isn't always so simple.

rows.title: How TikTok And Skater Girls Are Sending Skateboard Sales Off The Wall
rows.standfirst: The streets are full of skateboarders these days, and skate shops can hardly keep up with the demand. Why now? The answer might put a smile on your face.

rows.title: We Buy A Superhero 5: Hollywood
rows.standfirst: In the last and greatest chapter to our superhero saga, Micro-Face tries to make the jump from comic books to movies. | Subscribe to our weekly newsletter here.

rows.title: Flush With Cash, Americans Are Buying Everything From iPhones To Teslas
rows.standfirst: Personal income jumped by a record 21% last month, largely thanks to those $1,400 relief payments. The extra cash helped fuel a jump in spending that should continue in the months to come.

rows.title: Newsmax Issues Retraction And Apology To Dominion Employee Over Election Stories
rows.standfirst: Voting machine engineer Eric Coomer was falsely accused of rigging the election against former President Donald Trump by the conservative cable network. He faced death threats and has been in hiding.

rows.title: Shortages: Inflation In Disguise?
rows.standfirst: The pandemic spurred a year full of shortages, so why haven't producers responded by raising prices in most cases?

rows.title: Return For Mickey, Stay For The Churros: Disneyland Reopens After 13 Months
rows.standfirst: "I can't wait to just be there and feel it and listen to the music and smell the churros," says Robert Laird, a Disney megafan.

rows.title: 'Disaster Girl,' The Stuff Of Memes, Sells For Nearly $500,000 As NFT
rows.standfirst: Zoë Roth was just 4 when her dad took a picture of her standing in front a burning house. That photo launched uncounted memes, and now the original copy has sold at auction as a nonfungible token.

rows.title: What Makes President Biden's Massive Spending Pitch So Historic
rows.standfirst: Any one of President Biden's multi-trillion-dollar spending packages would be among the largest ever enacted by Congress. He has passed one — the American Recuse Plan — and proposed two others in his first 100 days.

rows.title: No College, No Problem. Some Employers Drop Degree Requirements To Diversify Staffs
rows.standfirst: More employers are focusing on skills rather than credentials, creating an opportunity for job candidates without college degrees to land positions.

rows.title: CVS To Offer In-Store Mental Health Counseling
rows.standfirst: As the number of people seeking therapy soars during the pandemic, CVS has begun testing a model to offer counseling services in its stores. It hopes to reduce costs for both patients and itself.

rows.title: Inflation, Unemployment And The Phillips Curve
rows.standfirst: For decades, policymakers chose to put millions of people into either a frying pan (inflation) or a fire (unemployment). An idea called the Phillips Curve was influential. But is it still?

rows.title: Germany's Small Business Owners Fight To Survive Amid Fears Of A Wave Of Insolvency
rows.standfirst: Germany's pandemic lockdowns have pushed thousands of small businesses toward insolvency. With a government freeze on insolvency rules soon expiring, some economists worry about what may happen next.

rows.title: Get Ready For A Shortage Of iPads And MacBooks
rows.standfirst: The global shortage of chips could hurt production of iPads and Macs, costing Apple $3 billion to $4 billion in revenue, in what is the latest example of a company being hit by supply constraints.

rows.title: FDA Moves To Ban Menthol Cigarettes And Flavored Cigars
rows.standfirst: Menthol has been the last allowable flavor in cigarettes, and the FDA says marginalized communities are far more likely to use these products.

rows.title: New York City, Former COVID-19 Epicenter, To 'Fully Reopen' On July 1
rows.standfirst: "This is going to be the summer of New York City," Mayor Bill de Blasio said, because people "want to live again." He cited the city's success in hitting or trending toward its reopening targets.

rows.title: Shopping And Shots Power An Economy Heading To Its Fastest Growth Since 1984
rows.standfirst: The U.S. economy grew at a rapid pace in the first three months of the year as more people got vaccinated and the federal government pumped hundreds of billions of dollars into people's pockets.
